drapeaux.note: Espagnol, titre du quotidien El Sol, 28 mai 1918, retraduit depuis le français

titre: The So-Called “Spanish” Flu, a Name Born of Censorship
accroche: In 1918, neutral Spain is the only country to publish its epidemic figures freely, and gives its name to a flu born elsewhere.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 28, 1918, the Madrid daily *El Sol* runs a front-page headline: “The Three-Day Fever — 80,000 Sick in Madrid — His Majesty the King Is Ill.” The news causes a sensation, all the more so because other European countries are going through the same epidemic at the same moment without a single newspaper saying a word about it. Spain has nothing special about it from a medical standpoint. It simply has the distinction, in the middle of World War I, of not being at war.

## A Neutrality That Speaks, Belligerents Who Stay Silent

Since 1914, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, and the United States have subjected their press to military censorship: announcing that an epidemic is weakening the troops or the home front would amount to informing the enemy about the country's morale. Newspapers in the belligerent countries therefore pass over the epidemic in silence, or barely mention it, even though it is spreading everywhere in Europe from the spring of 1918. Spain, neutral, has no reason to keep quiet: its press freely reports cases, overwhelmed hospitals, and even the illness of King Alfonso XIII. Seen from abroad, where the news circulates without the filter of censorship, Spain gives the impression of being the epicenter of the epidemic: simply because it is the only country talking about it.

A Spanish health official protests as early as October 1918, in a letter published in the *Journal of the American Medical Association*: he writes that he learned with surprise that the disease was ravaging other countries under the name “Spanish flu,” when it had not originated on Spanish soil. The true geographic origin is still debated today by researchers, who put forward Kansas (where a case is documented as early as March 1918 at Fort Riley military camp), northern France, or China, with no hypothesis commanding consensus.

## The Name That Outlived Its Own Error

The name “Spanish flu” never designated a geographic origin: it designates access to information. A century later, the pandemic that killed between 50 and 100 million people in its first year remains associated with the only country that had the misfortune, from the standpoint of its reputation, of not being at war, and therefore of not censoring its press. The shift matters beyond 1918: the name of an epidemic often says less about where it comes from than about who was first allowed to talk about it.

repere.texte: On May 28, 1918, the Madrid daily El Sol runs a headline about 80,000 sick in Madrid and the illness of King Alfonso XIII: three months before the belligerent countries officially admit to their own epidemics.

carte.punch: Spain did not invent the 1918 flu: it was just the only one to talk about it.
carte.idee: In 1918, wartime censorship keeps the French, British, German, and American press from reporting the epidemic spreading in their own countries. Only neutral Spain talks about it freely, to the point of making people abroad believe it is the epicenter.

quiz.question: Why was the 1918 flu called “Spanish”?
choix: Because the first confirmed cases had been recorded in Spain
Because the World Health Organization had officially named it that
Because the virus had first been identified in a Madrid laboratory
Because neutral Spain did not censor its press, unlike the countries at war
quiz.explication: The WHO did not yet exist in 1918 and no laboratory authenticated a Madrid origin; the first documented cases come from the United States (Kansas). The name comes from the fact that the uncensored Spanish press was the only one to talk about it freely.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Madrid daily El Sol report on May 28, 1918?
choix: The first confirmed case of the flu, identified in a Madrid military hospital
80,000 sick in Madrid and the illness of King Alfonso XIII, under the headline “The Three-Day Fever”
The death of King Alfonso XIII, carried off by the epidemic after several weeks of illness
A shortage of flu vaccines in Spanish public hospitals
quiz_supplementaire.explication: El Sol runs a headline about 80,000 sick in Madrid and the illness of King Alfonso XIII, news that causes a sensation while other countries live through the same epidemic in silence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does a Spanish health official react, in October 1918, to the name given to the epidemic?
choix: He demands financial compensation from other European countries for the damage to Spain's reputation
He proposes officially renaming the epidemic the “Kansas flu,” after its supposed origin
He protests in a letter published in the *Journal of the American Medical Association*, pointing out that the disease did not originate in Spain
He publishes a medical report proving that the virus was born in a Madrid laboratory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The official writes that he learned with surprise that other countries were ravaged by a disease they called Spanish flu, when it had not originated in Spain.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where do researchers place the real geographic origin of the 1918 pandemic, still without consensus today?
choix: In Kansas, northern France, or China, depending on the hypotheses put forward
In Spain itself, where the first documented cases date back to the winter of 1917
In Italy, in the trenches of the Austro-Italian front, according to a consensus established since the 2000s
In Russia, spread by soldiers returning from the Eastern Front after the 1917 revolution
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Researchers put forward several leads, Kansas, northern France, China, none of which commands consensus, the exact origin remaining debated.
